questions.prompt: A utility has 60,000 customers. An analyst phones 80 of them and finds that 35% would pay bills through an app. Which of these is the statistic?
options: The share of all 60,000 customers who would pay by app
The 35% found among the 80 customers phoned
The 80 customers who were phoned
The 60,000 customers of the utility
questions.explanation: A statistic is a number computed from the sample: the 35% among the 80. The share among all 60,000 is the parameter it estimates.
misconceptions: Names the parameter: the number that describes the whole population
Names the sample, which is a set of units, not a number
Names the population, which is a set of units, not a number

questions.prompt: An analyst draws 500 samples of 40 households and plots a histogram of the 500 sample means. What does one bar of this histogram count?
options: Households whose consumption falls in that range
Litres consumed by the households in that range
Samples whose mean falls in that range
Households that appear in more than one sample
questions.explanation: The histogram is a sampling distribution: each of its 500 entries is the mean of one sample.
misconceptions: Reads the sampling distribution as the distribution of households
Confuses the count on the vertical axis with the quantity on the horizontal axis
Invents a quantity the histogram does not show

questions.prompt: Two analysts each read 60 meters drawn at random from the same population, on the same day. One reports a mean of 452 litres, the other 489 litres. Both followed the method correctly. What explains the gap best?
options: Each sample is one draw of many, and means of 60 vary from draw to draw
One of the two samples must contain a recording error
The population mean must have changed in the time between the first sample and the second
Samples of 60 are too small to give any usable mean
questions.explanation: Two correctly drawn samples of 60 give two different means: the gap is ordinary sampling variation.
misconceptions: Treats sampling variation as a fault that needs a culprit
Reads a difference between samples as a change in the population
Overstates the problem: the mean is usable once its standard error is given

questions.prompt: A sample of 225 households has a mean consumption of 480 litres and a standard deviation of 180 litres. What is the estimated standard error of the mean?
options: 0.8 litres
12 litres
32 litres
180 litres
misconceptions: Divides the standard deviation by n and not by its square root
Divides the mean by the square root of n
Gives the standard deviation of households, which is not the error of the mean

questions.prompt: With 100 households the standard error of mean consumption is 20 litres. The manager wants a standard error of 5 litres. About how many households are needed?
options: 200 households
400 households
800 households
1,600 households
questions.explanation: The error must fall 4 times, which costs 4² = 16 times the sample: 1,600 households.
misconceptions: Assumes the error halves each time the sample doubles
Assumes the error falls in proportion to the sample
Doubles twice more than a proportional rule without squaring

questions.prompt: A report on 900 households says: "Mean consumption 465 litres (SD 210, SE 7)". A planner needs to know how much a single household can differ from the average. Which number answers the planner?
options: The SD, 210 litres
The SE, 7 litres
Twice the SE, 14 litres
The mean, 465 litres
questions.explanation: How far single households lie from the average is the standard deviation. The standard error describes the precision of the mean.
misconceptions: Applies the precision of the mean to single households
Builds an interval for the mean, which still says nothing about single households
Gives the centre, not the spread

questions.prompt: Complaint resolution times at a call centre have a median of 4 hours and a mean of 9 hours. What does that pair of numbers tell you about the distribution?
options: It is symmetric around 6.5 hours
It has a long tail of short resolutions
It has a long tail of long resolutions
It contains a calculation error
questions.explanation: A mean well above the median is the mark of a long right tail: a few very long resolutions pull the mean up.
misconceptions: Averages the two summaries as if neither were informative
Reverses the direction: a tail of small values would pull the mean below the median
Assumes mean and median must agree

questions.prompt: A sample of 99 repairs has a mean of 8.0 hours and a median of 6.0 hours. One more ticket of 808 hours is added. What happens to the two summaries, approximately?
options: Mean 8.1 hours, median 14 hours
Mean 16 hours, median 6 hours
Mean 16 hours, median 14 hours
Mean 8.1 hours, median 6 hours
questions.explanation: The new mean is (99 × 8 + 808) / 100 = 16 hours. The median only moves to a neighbouring ticket, so it stays near 6.
misconceptions: Swaps the behaviour of the two summaries
Lets the extreme value move the median as much as the mean
Assumes one value in a hundred cannot matter

questions.prompt: The finance team asks how many crew hours were paid for 3,000 repairs last quarter. The repair times are strongly skewed. Which summary should the analyst multiply by 3,000?
options: The median repair time
The trimmed mean repair time
The mean repair time
The most frequent repair time
questions.explanation: A total equals the mean times the count, whatever the shape of the distribution. The median times the count would understate the hours.
misconceptions: Uses the typical repair where a total is asked for
Drops the long repairs, whose hours were paid all the same
Uses the peak of the histogram, which ignores the tail entirely

questions.prompt: A sample of waiting times has first quartile 12 minutes, median 20 minutes and third quartile 34 minutes. What is the interquartile range?
options: 8 minutes
14 minutes
20 minutes
22 minutes
questions.explanation: The interquartile range is the third quartile minus the first: 34 - 12 = 22 minutes.
misconceptions: Takes the median minus the first quartile
Takes the third quartile minus the median
Gives the median itself

questions.prompt: An analyst summarises 250 skewed repair times, three of which are tickets closed weeks late. Which sentence gives a reader what is needed to rely on the summary?
options: Repairs took 11 hours on average, give or take 40
Of 250 sampled repairs the median was 6 hours and the quartiles 4 and 10; 3 late tickets are listed apart
The typical repair at the utility takes 6 hours
After cleaning, the mean repair time was 7 hours
questions.explanation: It gives the count, the middle, the spread and the exclusion, and claims nothing beyond the sample.
misconceptions: Uses mean and standard deviation on skewed data, with a range that goes below zero
Gives no count, no spread and states a sample result as a fact about all repairs
Hides what "cleaning" removed, so the number cannot be checked

questions.prompt: A table of median repair time by district is built from a sample of 300 repairs. District D30 has 4 repairs in the sample and the highest median of all. What should the analyst do with that row?
options: Report it as the worst district
Withhold the number and state that the count is too small
Replace it with the overall median
Delete the district from the table without a note
questions.explanation: A median of 4 tickets is unstable and, in a small district, can point at single households. The row is withheld with the reason stated.
misconceptions: Ranks on a number that four tickets cannot support
Invents a value the data did not give
Removes the row in silence, so the reader cannot tell it was ever there

questions.prompt: An analyst has 120 call durations and bootstraps their median. Why is each resample drawn with replacement?
options: So that resamples differ from one another the way real samples would
So that each resample is larger than the original sample
So that extreme durations are removed from the resamples
So that every one of the 120 durations appears exactly once in each resample
questions.explanation: Drawing 120 from 120 without replacement returns the same sample every time. Replacement makes the resamples vary, which imitates sampling from the population.
misconceptions: Confuses replacement with a change of size: a resample has the size of the sample
Believes the bootstrap cleans the data; it reuses every value as it is
Describes sampling without replacement, which gives identical resamples

questions.prompt: From 1,000 bootstrap medians, sorted from smallest to largest, an analyst wants the 90% percentile interval. Which two sorted values are its ends?
options: The 25th and the 975th
The 50th and the 950th
The 100th and the 900th
The 1st and the 1,000th
questions.explanation: A 90% interval leaves 5% in each tail: 5% of 1,000 is 50, so the 50th and the 950th values.
misconceptions: Gives the ends of the 95% interval
Leaves 10% in each tail, which is an 80% interval
Takes the full range of the resamples, which grows with their number

questions.prompt: A bootstrap interval for a median from 90 tickets is 4.8 to 7.9 hours with 2,000 resamples. The manager finds it too wide. Which action would narrow it?
options: Raising the resamples to 200,000
Reporting the 99% interval instead
Collecting more tickets
Resampling 45 tickets at a time
questions.explanation: The width is set by the information in the sample. Only more data narrow it; more resamples only steady the same interval.
misconceptions: Confuses the number of resamples with the sample size
A higher level makes the interval wider, not narrower
Smaller resamples vary more, which widens the interval and no longer matches the study

questions.prompt: A consultant reports "a 95% interval for the mean bill: 212 to 236 riyals". Which statement describes what the 95% refers to?
options: 95% of all customers of the company have a monthly bill somewhere between 212 and 236 riyals
The interval was computed from 95% of the customers
The method produces intervals that contain the true mean in about 95 of 100 studies
The sample mean is 95% of the true mean
questions.explanation: The level is the coverage of the method over repeated studies.
misconceptions: Reads an interval for a mean as a range for single customers
Confuses the level with the share of data used
Invents a relation between the level and the size of the estimate

questions.prompt: To check an interval method, an analyst simulates 400 studies from a known population. In 368 of them the 95% interval contains the true value. What coverage did the method deliver?
questions.explanation: 368 / 400 = 0.92. The method promised 95% and delivered 92% on this population.
misconceptions: Divides by a wrong total
Reports the promise in place of the count
Adds the shortfall instead of subtracting it

questions.prompt: Claim payments at an insurer are mostly small, but about one claim in 2,000 is larger than all the others in a typical month together. An analyst bootstraps the mean payment from 150 claims. What should a coverage check be expected to show?
options: Coverage near 95%, because the bootstrap needs no assumption about the shape of the data
Coverage far below 95%, because most samples contain no very large claim
Coverage above 95%, because the intervals are very wide
Coverage of exactly 95%, because 150 is a large sample
questions.explanation: A sample without a rare huge claim has no information about it, so its interval for the mean sits too low. The bootstrap can only reuse what the sample holds.
misconceptions: Believes "no assumption" means "always valid": the sample must still represent the population
Expects wide intervals, but samples without a huge claim give narrow ones
Treats a fixed sample size as a guarantee whatever the shape of the data

questions.prompt: A study weighs 10 loaves from each of 30 bakeries chosen at random, 300 loaves in all, to estimate the mean weight of a loaf in the city. Which unit should a bootstrap resample?
options: The loaf
The bakery, with its 10 loaves
The weighing scale
Half of the loaves of each bakery
questions.explanation: Bakeries were drawn at random and loaves of one bakery resemble each other, so the bakery is the unit.
misconceptions: Treats 300 loaves as independent although they come in groups of 10
Names a tool, not a sampled unit
Keeps all 30 bakeries in every resample, so the variation between bakeries is never imitated

questions.prompt: An analyst bootstraps rows of a two-stage survey (8 districts, 50 households each) and gets a 95% interval 0.3 points wide. A colleague resamples districts and gets 0.8 points. A simulation on a known population shows coverages of 61% and 93%. Which interval should be reported, and why?
options: The narrow one, because it is more precise
The narrow one, because it uses all 400 rows and so wastes none of the information
The wide one, because its method keeps the promise of 95% most nearly
Neither, because the two methods disagree
questions.explanation: An interval is judged by its coverage. The row bootstrap ignores that districts were sampled and misses the truth in 39% of studies.
misconceptions: Mistakes a narrow interval for a good one: narrow and wrong is worse than wide and right
Both bootstraps use all rows; the difference is the unit, not the amount of data
Disagreement is the finding: one method matches the design and one does not

questions.prompt: A file holds 600 satisfaction scores. Before bootstrapping, what does the analyst most need to find out?
options: Whether the scores are whole numbers
How the 600 respondents were selected
Which software collected the scores
Whether the file is sorted by score
questions.explanation: The resampling unit follows from the sampling design: respondents picked one by one, or in groups such as districts or branches.
misconceptions: Looks at the format of the values, which does not decide the unit
Looks at the tool, which says nothing about independence
Sorting does not change a bootstrap, which draws rows at random

questions.prompt: Median delivery time is 40 minutes for courier X and 46 minutes for courier Y. A bootstrap gives a 95% interval for the ratio Y / X of 0.97 to 1.36. What can be said?
options: Y is slower by between 3% and 36%
Y may be anywhere from 3% faster to 36% slower
Y is slower by 15%, with certainty
The two couriers are equally fast
questions.explanation: The interval for the ratio includes 1, the value of no gap, and runs from 0.97 (3% faster) to 1.36 (36% slower).
misconceptions: Reads 0.97 as "3% slower": a ratio below 1 means faster
Drops the interval and treats the estimate as exact
Reads "includes 1" as proof of equality

questions.prompt: A study has 150 repairs by crew A and 90 by crew B. An analyst pools the 240 repairs, resamples 240 with replacement, splits them by crew label and takes the difference of medians. What is wrong with this bootstrap for the study as designed?
options: It draws with replacement, which a difference between two groups does not allow in any bootstrap
It lets the number of repairs per crew change from resample to resample
It uses medians, which cannot be bootstrapped
It resamples too few repairs
questions.explanation: The study fixed 150 and 90. Resampling the pool makes the group sizes random; each crew should be resampled on its own.
misconceptions: Replacement is what every bootstrap uses
Medians bootstrap well at these sizes
The resample has the size of the study, as it should

questions.prompt: A dashboard shows a 95% interval for branch A, 6.1 to 7.4, and for branch B, 7.0 to 8.6. They overlap. A manager concludes that the branches do not differ. What is the sound next step?
options: Accept the conclusion, because overlapping intervals mean no difference
Build the interval for the difference between the branches
Widen both intervals to 99% and look again
Compare the two lower ends only
questions.explanation: Overlap of two separate intervals is not a test. The interval for the difference itself can exclude zero even when the two intervals overlap.
misconceptions: Uses the overlap rule of thumb, which is too conservative
Wider intervals overlap more and answer nothing
Looks at one end of each interval, which is not a comparison

questions.prompt: Two call scripts were given to callers at random. To test the difference in mean call length, an analyst shuffles the script labels 5,000 times. What question do the 5,000 shuffled differences answer?
options: How large a difference arises when the script has no effect
How large the true effect of the new script on call length is in the population
How long calls would be with a third script
How many callers received the wrong script
questions.explanation: Shuffled labels carry no information about call length, so the shuffled differences show what chance alone produces.
misconceptions: Expects an effect size from a procedure that assumes there is no effect
Asks about a condition that was never observed
Mistakes the shuffle for an audit of the assignment

questions.prompt: The observed difference in means is 1.8 minutes. Among 4,999 shuffles, 149 give a difference of 1.8 minutes or more in either direction. Counting the observed arrangement as one more shuffle, what is the two-sided p-value?
misconceptions: Divides by ten times too many shuffles
Halves the count as if the test were one-sided
Misplaces the decimal point

questions.prompt: A pilot compares the 90th percentile of waiting time between two service desks, 25 customers each. No standard formula for this comparison is at hand. Which approach gives a valid p-value?
options: A t-test on the two means, with the result reported as a test of the 90th percentiles
A comparison of the two bootstrap intervals by eye
The larger of the two percentiles divided by the smaller
A permutation test with the difference in 90th percentiles as its statistic
questions.explanation: A permutation test works for any statistic: shuffle the desk labels, recompute the difference in 90th percentiles, and count.
misconceptions: Tests a different quantity from the one asked about
Overlap of two intervals is not a test
Gives an effect size and no measure of chance

questions.prompt: A report states: "The new reminder letter reduced late payment (p = 0.02)." Which sentence says correctly what the 0.02 is?
options: There is a 2% chance that the letter has no effect and a 98% chance that it reduced late payment by some amount
The letter reduced late payment by 2%
If the letter had no effect, a reduction at least this large would appear in about 2 studies of 100
In 2% of customers the letter did not work
questions.explanation: A p-value is computed under the assumption of no effect: it is the share of such worlds with a result at least this extreme.
misconceptions: Reads the p-value as the probability of the null hypothesis
Reads the p-value as an effect size
Reads the p-value as a share of customers

questions.prompt: A trial with 18 pumps per group finds no significant difference in failures between two lubricants (p = 0.45). The maintenance lead writes: "The lubricants are equivalent." What is the weakness of that sentence?
options: A study this small would often give a large p-value even if one lubricant were clearly better
A p-value of 0.45 means the lubricants differ in 45% of pumps
The p-value should have been compared with 0.5, not 0.05
Significance cannot be tested at all with fewer than 30 units per group, so the p-value is not valid
questions.explanation: A large p-value from a small study is absence of evidence. The interval for the difference would show how large a gap is still possible.
misconceptions: Reads the p-value as a share of units
Invents a threshold
States a rule of thumb as a law; small groups can be tested, with low power

questions.prompt: A team screens 200 ideas for reducing leaks. Experience says about 10 of 200 really work. Each is tested at the 0.05 level with a study that detects a working idea 60% of the time. About how many of the "significant" ideas are false alarms?
options: About 5% of them
About 20% of them
About 40% of them
About 60% of them
questions.explanation: False alarms: 190 × 0.05 ≈ 9.5. True detections: 10 × 0.6 = 6. So about 9.5 of 15.5 significant results, roughly 60%, are false.
misconceptions: Takes the 0.05 level for the share of false alarms among significant results
Guesses between the level and the truth without counting
Uses the share of misses among working ideas

questions.prompt: A new routing rule changes mean travel time per repair by -6 minutes (95% interval -9 to -3). Operations say that a saving of at least 5 minutes pays for the rule. How should the result be reported?
options: A real saving; whether it reaches 5 minutes is not settled
A real saving of more than 5 minutes
No saving was shown
A real saving that is too small to matter
questions.explanation: The interval excludes 0 and includes the threshold of 5 minutes: the saving is real, and it may be 3 or 9 minutes.
misconceptions: Reads the estimate and ignores that the interval reaches down to 3 minutes
Ignores that the interval excludes zero
Ignores that the interval reaches beyond the threshold

questions.prompt: Satisfaction scores have a standard deviation of 2.0 points in both of two regions. The regions differ by 0.5 points in mean score. What is the standardised effect size d?
questions.explanation: d is the difference divided by the standard deviation: 0.5 / 2.0 = 0.25.
misconceptions: Divides by the square of the standard deviation and rounds
Divides by 2.5 instead of 2.0
Divides the standard deviation by the difference

questions.prompt: A simulation shows that a planned survey of 150 customers per group would detect a true gap of 0.3 points in 35% of studies. The survey is run and finds p = 0.21. What can be concluded about a gap of 0.3 points?
options: It is ruled out, because the result is not significant and the survey was planned with a simulation
It is confirmed, because the power was low
It is half as likely as before the survey
It remains plausible, because the survey would have missed it about two times in three
questions.explanation: With 35% power the survey says "not significant" in 65% of the worlds where the gap is real, so a non-significant result barely speaks against it.
misconceptions: Reads a non-significant result from a weak study as proof of no gap
Turns low power into evidence for the effect
Invents a probability the analysis does not provide

questions.prompt: A dashboard tests 60 branches against the company average each month at the 0.05 level. In a month in which no branch truly differs, about how many branches will be flagged?
questions.explanation: 60 × 0.05 = 3 false flags are expected when nothing differs.
misconceptions: Assumes that a 5% test gives no flags when nothing differs
Uses 10% in place of 5%
Uses 20% in place of 5%

questions.prompt: Five tests give the p-values 0.004, 0.011, 0.020, 0.030 and 0.400. Holm's method at 0.05 compares the smallest with 0.05/5, the next with 0.05/4, and so on, and stops at the first failure. How many hypotheses does it reject?
questions.explanation: 0.004 < 0.010 passes; 0.011 < 0.0125 passes; 0.020 < 0.0167 fails, so Holm stops with 2 rejections.
misconceptions: Compares every p-value with 0.05/5
Rejects every p-value below 0.05, with no correction
Rejects all five because the smallest passed

questions.prompt: A league table ranks 40 clinics by the share of patients seen within the target time. The five best and the five worst are all among the smallest clinics. Before any clinic is praised or inspected, what is the most likely explanation to check?
options: Small clinics are managed either very well or very badly, with little in between, unlike large ones
Small clinics report their data less carefully
The target is unfair to clinics of middle size
Shares based on few patients vary most, so small clinics land at both ends by chance
questions.explanation: An estimate from few cases has a large standard error, so the extremes of a ranking are filled by the smallest units whatever their true performance.
misconceptions: Explains by management a pattern that sampling variation produces unaided
Proposes a data-quality cause without evidence when a simpler one exists
Blames the target for a pattern that is about sample size

questions.prompt: An analyst compares two billing layouts on complaint rates and finds nothing. She then splits customers by region, by age band and by tariff, and reports the one split in which the layouts differ at p = 0.04. No correction is applied. What is the problem with the reported result?
options: It is the best of many looks, so its p-value overstates the evidence
A p-value of 0.04 is too close to 0.05 to count
Complaint rates cannot be compared between subgroups of customers of different size
The subgroups were too large for a test
questions.explanation: Each split is another test. The smallest of many p-values is often below 0.05 when nothing differs, so the plan and the number of looks must be reported.
misconceptions: Treats closeness to the level as the defect, when the defect is the number of looks
Subgroups can be compared; the looks have to be counted
Size is not the issue here; selection after seeing the data is

questions.prompt: A screening of 500 pipe segments flags candidates for a cheap follow-up inspection. The team can accept that about one flag in ten is a false alarm, and wants to miss as few faulty segments as possible. Which procedure fits that aim?
options: No correction at all, because the follow-up inspections are cheap and false alarms therefore cost little
Holm at 0.05, because it is the strictest
One test of all 500 segments together
Benjamini-Hochberg at 10%, which limits the share of false alarms among the flags
questions.explanation: The stated tolerance is a share of false flags, which is what the false discovery rate controls. Holm guards against even one false flag and would miss more faulty segments.
misconceptions: With 500 tests and no correction the false flags are not held to one in ten
Controls a stricter promise than the team asked for, at the cost of missed faults
Says whether something differs somewhere and names no segment

questions.prompt: Electricity use of 800 flats is regressed on the number of rooms: use = 150 + 210 × rooms, in kilowatt-hours a month. A planner asks how much more a five-room flat uses than a three-room flat, on average. What does the line say?
options: 420 kilowatt-hours a month more
210 kilowatt-hours a month more
570 kilowatt-hours a month more
1,200 kilowatt-hours a month more
questions.explanation: Two more rooms at 210 kilowatt-hours each: 2 × 210 = 420. The intercept cancels in a difference.
misconceptions: Gives the slope for one room when the flats differ by two
Adds the intercept to a difference, where it cancels
Gives the predicted use of a five-room flat, not the difference

questions.prompt: Fuel use of delivery vans is regressed on the load carried, for loads between 200 and 900 kilograms: litres per 100 km = 7.5 + 0.004 × load. A colleague uses the line to budget fuel for a lorry carrying 12,000 kilograms. What is the main objection?
options: The slope has no units and cannot be multiplied by a load
The intercept of 7.5 shows that the line is biased
The load is far outside the range the line was fitted on, where nothing shows the relation still holds
A fitted line can be used only to describe the vans it was fitted on and never to predict the fuel use of any vehicle
questions.explanation: The data stop at 900 kilograms. A lorry is another kind of vehicle, and the line has no evidence about it.
misconceptions: The slope has units: litres per 100 km for each kilogram
An intercept above zero is what an empty van would be expected to use
Prediction inside the observed range is a sound use of a fitted line

questions.prompt: A survey of 3,000 employees finds that each additional training day taken last year goes with 1.8 more points on the performance review. A report concludes: "Sending an employee on one more training day will raise the review by 1.8 points." Which objection is the strongest?
options: The sample of 3,000 is too small for a slope
A slope cannot be estimated for a count such as days
The slope should have been reported per hour of training and not per day, since days differ in length
Employees who take more training may differ in other ways that also raise reviews
questions.explanation: The survey compares different employees. Motivation, role or manager may go with both training and reviews, so the slope is not the effect of sending one person.
misconceptions: 3,000 employees give a precise slope; precision is not the problem
Counts are ordinary predictors in a regression
A change of units rescales the slope and changes nothing about its meaning

questions.prompt: Two analysts each draw 500 customers at random from the same billing system and regress bill on consumption. One finds a slope of 2.31 riyals per cubic metre, the other 2.42. Neither made an error. What explains the two values?
options: A slope computed from a sample varies from sample to sample, like a mean
The tariff changed between the two draws
One of the two used the wrong formula
Least squares gives a different answer each time it runs on the same data
questions.explanation: A fitted slope is a statistic. It has a sampling distribution and a standard error, like every estimate in this course.
misconceptions: Invents a cause when sampling variation is enough
Assumes that different results mean a mistake
Least squares is deterministic: the same data always give the same line

questions.prompt: To bootstrap the slope of salary on years of experience for 600 employees, an analyst resamples the experience column and the salary column separately, each with replacement. The bootstrap slopes come out close to zero. Why?
options: Too few resamples were drawn
Salaries are skewed, which a bootstrap cannot handle
Separate resampling breaks the link between each employee's two values
The slope of the original sample was itself close to zero
questions.explanation: The unit is the employee. Drawing the two columns separately pairs one person's experience with another person's salary, which removes the relation.
misconceptions: The number of resamples changes the steadiness of the result, not its centre
A pairs bootstrap makes no assumption about the shape of the data
The original slope was not near zero; the resampling destroyed it

questions.prompt: In a regression of monthly sales on shop floor area, the residuals scatter within about 5,000 riyals for small shops and within about 40,000 riyals for large ones. What does this do to the output of the default formula?
options: It biases the slope upward
It makes the reported R² meaningless as a description of the fit
It makes the reported p-value too large
It makes the reported standard error of the slope too small
questions.explanation: Unequal spread leaves the slope a fair estimate. The default standard error assumes one spread everywhere, and it understates the uncertainty when the noisiest points sit at the end of the line.
misconceptions: Unequal spread does not bias the least-squares slope
R² still describes how closely the points follow the line
A standard error that is too small makes p-values too small, not too large

questions.prompt: On a known population, an analyst draws 400 samples and builds two 95% intervals for a slope in each. The formula interval contains the true slope in 352 samples, the bootstrap interval in 381. What do the counts show?
options: Coverage of 88% and 95%: the bootstrap interval keeps the promise and the formula interval does not
Coverage of 95% for both, since both are 95% intervals
Coverage of 12% and 5%: both intervals fail
Coverage cannot be judged from 400 samples, since a count from so few samples is itself too uncertain to compare
questions.explanation: 352 / 400 = 88% and 381 / 400 = 95.25%. Coverage is counted, and the nominal level is only a promise.
misconceptions: Takes the label of the interval for its measured coverage
Reports the miss rates as if they were coverage
400 samples give coverage to within about two points, enough to separate 88% from 95%

questions.prompt: A regression table shows for the variable "distance_km": coefficient 0.85, standard error 0.10, p < 0.001. The outcome is delivery time in minutes. Which sentence reports the result best?
options: Distance is a highly significant predictor of delivery time (p < 0.001), so the routing model is confirmed
The coefficient of distance is 0.85 with a standard error of 0.10
Each additional kilometre goes with about 0.85 minutes more (95% interval about 0.65 to 1.05)
Distance explains 85% of delivery time
questions.explanation: The coefficient in units, with its interval: 0.85 ± 2 × 0.10. The p-value answers "is the slope zero", which nobody asked.
misconceptions: Reports the test and leaves out the size
Repeats the table without units or an interval
Reads a coefficient as a share of variation explained

questions.prompt: Hospital stay in days is regressed on the number of medicines prescribed: 0.9 days per medicine. When the severity of the illness is added to the model, the slope on medicines falls to 0.2. What is the most likely reason?
options: Severely ill patients get more medicines and also stay longer for other reasons
The first model had too few patients
Adding any second variable to a regression model always lowers the slopes of the variables already in it
Severity was measured with error
questions.explanation: Severity is tied to both the number of medicines and the stay. Left out, its share of the stay was credited to medicines.
misconceptions: Blames sampling error for a change that comes from asking a different question
A variable unrelated to medicines would have left the slope where it was
Measurement error in severity would have left more of the confounding in place, not produced the drop

questions.prompt: After regressing energy use of buildings on floor area, an analyst plots the residuals against the age of the building, a variable that is not in the model. The residuals rise steadily with age. What does the plot indicate?
options: The slope on floor area is too large to be real
Age should be removed from the dataset
Age carries systematic information about energy use that the model is missing
The residuals were computed wrongly, since they should always average zero
questions.explanation: A trend of residuals against a variable left out means that the variable explains part of what the model missed.
misconceptions: The plot is about what is missing, not about the size of the fitted slope
A variable that explains the outcome is a reason to use it, not to drop it
Residuals average zero overall and can still trend against another variable

questions.prompt: A model of water use gives 98 litres per person with household size alone, and 86 litres per person once area temperature is included. A planner sizes the supply for one new scheme, in one area, for families of different sizes. Which figure fits her question?
options: 98, because it comes from the simpler model
92, the average of the two
Neither, because the two models contradict each other
86, because within one area the temperature does not change
questions.explanation: Her comparison is between families in the same area, which is what "holding temperature fixed" describes.
misconceptions: Simplicity does not make a slope answer a question it was not built for
Averages two answers to two different questions
The models answer different questions; they do not contradict

questions.prompt: After adding three more variables, an analyst writes: "All confounders are now controlled, so the slope is the causal effect." What is the weakness of the sentence?
options: Three variables are too many for one model
A slope is never related to a cause
Controlling for more variables always makes a slope less precise, so the estimate has lost its value as evidence
Only the measured variables were adjusted for; one that nobody measured may still be mixed in
questions.explanation: A regression adjusts for what is in the model. Only assignment by chance protects against the variables nobody thought of.
misconceptions: A model with a few thousand rows carries three more variables easily
Overstates the limit: with assignment by chance a slope can estimate an effect
Often true, and beside the point of the claim

questions.prompt: A manager asks: "Are customers happier with the new app?" Which line turns the question into an estimand?
options: The difference in mean satisfaction score between app users and other customers surveyed this quarter
A permutation test with 5,000 shuffles
Whether the app is good
The satisfaction scores of all customers in the survey file for this quarter, with a column that marks the app users
questions.explanation: An estimand names one quantity, the population and the two groups compared.
misconceptions: Names a method, not the quantity to be estimated
Restates the question without a quantity or a population
Names the data, not a number to estimate

questions.prompt: An analyst must put an interval on the share of 350 sampled invoices that were paid late, and has only the bootstrap code written for a mean. What is the sound way forward?
options: Wait for a method specific to shares
Bootstrap the median payment delay instead
Code each invoice 1 if late and 0 if not, and bootstrap the mean of that column
Report the share with no interval, since shares are exact
questions.explanation: A share is the mean of a column of zeros and ones, so the bootstrap for a mean applies unchanged.
misconceptions: Assumes each statistic needs its own recipe
Answers a different question from the one asked
A share from a sample has sampling error like any estimate

questions.prompt: Four closing sentences are proposed for a brief on repair times drawn from one year of logged tickets. Which one states a limit a manager can use?
options: These results rest on a sample and on logged data, and they should therefore be interpreted with a suitable degree of caution
More research is needed
Statistics can never prove anything
Tickets closed late in the system count as slow repairs, so the true share within the standard may be higher
questions.explanation: A useful limit names what could be wrong and in which direction.
misconceptions: A ritual sentence that names no specific risk
Says nothing about what is uncertain here
A general remark that would fit any study

questions.prompt: A draft reads: "Mean resolution time fell from 31 to 27 hours after the new rule (p = 0.03), so the rule works." The data are complaints from the month before and the month after the change. What must be added before a manager acts on it?
options: An interval for the 4-hour change, and the limit that the two months may differ for other reasons
A second p-value from another test, such as a classical test, to confirm that the first one was computed correctly
More decimal places for the two means
The number of resamples used
questions.explanation: The size needs an interval, and a before-and-after comparison cannot separate the rule from anything else that changed between the months.
misconceptions: A second test adds no information about size or design
Precision of printing is not precision of the estimate
A method detail that belongs in the notebook

questions.prompt: Zulal surveys customer satisfaction. To report on its 200 commercial customers it phones 100 of them, and it phones 300 of its 40,000 residential customers at random. Commercial customers score 5.0 on average in the sample, residential 7.0. What estimate of mean satisfaction over all 40,200 customers follows from the design?
options: 6.5, the mean of all 400 responses
6.0, the mean of the two group means
5.5, because the commercial customers were drawn more carefully and so count for more
About 7.0, each group weighted by its N / n
questions.explanation: Each commercial response stands for 2 customers and each residential one for about 133. Weighted, the residential group dominates: (200 × 5.0 + 40,000 × 7.0) / 40,200 is about 6.99.
misconceptions: Counts every row the same, so the oversampled group gets a quarter of the weight instead of half a percent
Gives the two groups equal weight although one is 200 times larger
Confuses the care of the design with the size of the group it stands for

questions.prompt: Ilyas ranks the 30 districts by a quarterly complaint rate and sends a support team to the five worst. Next quarter their rate falls by a third, and Nizar wants to roll the team out everywhere. Most of the five are small districts. What should Ilyas say first?
options: The fall is real, because it is large and happened in all five districts at once
The team works only if a before-and-after test on the five gives p below 0.05
Compare the five with the five best districts over the same quarter
Part of the fall is expected anyway; compare with equally bad districts left out by lot
questions.explanation: Districts picked for being extreme, especially small ones, are partly extreme by chance and drift back next quarter. A concurrent comparison among equally extreme districts, assigned by lot, regresses the same way on both sides and isolates the team's effect.
misconceptions: Takes the size and consistency of the fall as proof, although selection on extremes produces both
A significant before-and-after test still credits regression to the mean to the team
The best districts drift down as the worst drift up, so this comparison doubles the bias instead of removing it

questions.prompt: A meter-fault flag is checked on 200 faulty meters and 200 sound ones: it flags 180 faulty and 20 sound, a precision of 90% on the set. In the region 2% of meters are faulty. What share of flagged meters will be faulty in the field?
options: 90%, the precision measured on the balanced set of 400 meters
50%, the share of faulty meters among the 400 that were checked
About 16%, once each class is weighted back
2%, the share of faulty meters in the region as a whole
questions.explanation: Sensitivity 0.9 and false-alarm rate 0.1 carry over; the mix does not. 0.9 × 0.02 / (0.9 × 0.02 + 0.1 × 0.98) is about 0.155.
misconceptions: Treats precision as a property of the flag, although it depends on how common faults are
Reads the prevalence from a set whose mix the analyst fixed at half and half
Forgets that the flag raises the share above the base rate by selecting likely faults
